faqs.question: How many 80lb bags of concrete are in a cubic yard?
faqs.answer: There are exactly 45 bags of 80lb pre-mixed concrete in one cubic yard. One 80lb bag yields 0.60 cubic feet of mixed concrete, and 27 cubic feet (1 cubic yard) divided by 0.60 cu ft per bag equals 45 bags (before adding waste margins).

faqs.question: How many tons of gravel are in a cubic yard?
faqs.answer: There are approximately 1.4 short US tons (2,800 lbs) of crushed gravel or stone in one cubic yard based on standard loose aggregate density (1.40 tons per cu yd). Dense aggregates like crushed granite may reach 1.5 to 1.6 tons per cubic yard.

faqs.question: How much extra concrete, gravel, or framing material should I order for waste?
faqs.answer: Industry standard practice is to order a 10% material waste margin. For concrete, this accounts for uneven sub-grade depth and form flex; for gravel, it covers compaction shrinkage (10%–15%); and for lumber and drywall, it compensates for cuts, headers, and scrap.

faqs.question: How do I calculate how many studs I need for a framing wall?
faqs.answer: To calculate wall studs, convert wall length to inches and divide by stud spacing (16" or 24" on-center), then add 1 end stud. Next, add 2 extra studs per corner or wall intersection, plus double studs for window or door headers, and apply a 10% waste buffer.

faqs.question: How do I calculate how many drywall sheets I need for a room?
faqs.answer: Calculate total surface area by multiplying wall perimeter by ceiling height, plus room length by width if including the ceiling. Divide total square footage by sheet coverage (32 sq ft for a 4x8 sheet or 48 sq ft for a 4x12 sheet), then add a 10% waste margin for window and door cutouts. A complete drywall estimate includes approx 32 feet of paper joint tape, 32 drywall screws, and 0.05 lbs of joint compound mud per square foot (Level 4 finish standard).

methodologyPage.title: Methodology & Trade Sources
methodologyPage.subtitle: We believe in transparency. Build Yardage calculators are engineered to eliminate guesswork by adhering to rigorous geometric math and established building codes. Below are the governing standards and logic applied across our platform.
methodologyPage.concreteMethodology: Standard volumetric geometry (Length × Width × Depth for slabs; π × r² × Height for columns). A strict conversion factor of 27 cubic feet per cubic yard is applied. Bag yield estimates are based on industry-standard pre-mix weights (80lb = 0.60 cu ft yield).
methodologyPage.concreteReference: ACI 332 (Residential Concrete Code) for recommended waste margins and standard volumetric math. Note: Our prior generic 'ASTM C94' badge was removed as C94 governs ready-mix delivery, not dimensional geometry.
methodologyPage.gravelMethodology: Volumetric geometry converted to tonnage using a canonical loose aggregate density factor of 1.4 tons per cubic yard (2,800 lbs/yd³). This reflects the as-delivered weight from the quarry before in-place compaction.
methodologyPage.gravelReference: ASTM D2940 (Standard Specification for Graded Aggregate Material for Bases) and industry-standard loose density factors.
methodologyPage.drywallMethodology: Surface area divided by sheet size (32 sq ft for 4x8). Fastener and compound rates are strictly governed by canonical industry rates: 32 screws per 4x8 sheet (for 16" O.C. framing), 32 ft of tape per sheet, and 0.05 lbs of joint compound per square foot.
methodologyPage.drywallReference: ASTM C840 / Gypsum Association GA-216 (Application and Finishing of Gypsum Board).
methodologyPage.framingMethodology: Field studs are calculated by wall length divided by O.C. spacing. We account for structural depth by adding specific material for corners (3-stud conventional or 2-stud advanced) and openings (2 kings + 2 jacks per door/window), while deducting the interrupted field studs spanning the opening width.
methodologyPage.framingReference: IRC 2021 Section R602 (Wall Framing Provisions) & NDS (National Design Specification for Wood Construction).
methodologyPage.rebarMethodology: Calculates linear footage required for a matrix based on length, width, edge clearance, and grid spacing. Lap splices are dynamically calculated per bar size using the standard 40d (40 × bar diameter) multiplier.
methodologyPage.rebarReference: ACI 318 §25.5 (Building Code Requirements for Structural Concrete - Lap Splices) & CRSI Manual of Standard Practice.
